questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes isotopes from isobars?

options.option_text: Isotopes have the same mass number; isobars share the same atomic number
Isotopes share the same atomic number; isobars have the same mass number
Isotopes have equal neutron counts; isobars have equal proton counts only
Isotopes and isobars both carry an identical total number of electrons

questions.explanation: B is correct: isotopes belong to the same element (same atomic number, same protons) but differ in neutron count, giving different mass numbers. Isobars are atoms of different elements sharing the same mass number. Option A is the classic reversal error — swapping 'atomic number' and 'mass number' — which is the most frequently tested distractor in SSC/IBPS papers.

questions.stem: Which experimental observation in J.J. Thomson's cathode ray tube directly indicated that cathode rays carry negative charge?

options.option_text: Cathode rays produced green fluorescence on a zinc sulfide-coated screen
Cathode rays deflected toward the positively charged plate in an electric field
Cathode rays traveled in perfectly straight lines when no field was applied
Cathode rays had the same charge-to-mass ratio regardless of the cathode material

questions.explanation: B is correct: deflection toward the positive plate proves the rays carry negative charge (opposite charges attract). Option A (fluorescence) only confirmed energy transfer, not charge sign. Option D, though a real Thomson finding, established the universality of electrons — it did not directly indicate negative charge.

questions.stem: A student assigns quantum numbers n=2, l=2, ml=0, ms=−½ to an electron. Why is this set invalid?

options.option_text: The magnetic quantum number ml cannot be zero for any l=2 orbital
The azimuthal quantum number l must be less than the principal quantum number n
The spin quantum number ms must equal +½ whenever the ml value equals zero
Electrons sharing the same ml value must also share the same ms value

questions.explanation: B is correct: l ranges from 0 to (n−1). For n=2, l can only be 0 or 1; l=2 is forbidden. Option A is wrong — ml=0 is perfectly valid for l=2 (one of five d-orbital orientations). Option C inverts the Pauli rule and is chemically meaningless.

questions.stem: The ground-state electronic configuration of Chromium (Cr, Z=24) is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than the expected [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². What is the primary reason for this deviation from the Aufbau principle?

options.option_text: The 3d⁵ 4s¹ arrangement minimises electron-electron repulsion within the 4s orbital
A half-filled 3d subshell (3d⁵) confers extra stability through exchange energy
The 4s orbital energy rises above 3d level for all elements beyond Z=20 generally
Shielding by inner electrons forces one 4s electron to migrate into the 3d set

questions.explanation: B is correct: half-filled subshells (3d⁵ with one electron per orbital) gain stabilisation via maximum exchange energy — a quantum mechanical effect. Option A conflates orbital repulsion with subshell stability. Option C is a partial truth about d-block energetics but does not explain why exactly 3d⁵ 4s¹ is preferred over 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.stem: A proton and an alpha particle are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V. The ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths (λ_proton : λ_alpha) is?

options.option_text: 1 : 1, since both particles gain energy from the same potential difference V
2√2 : 1, as proton's lower mass and charge yield a longer de Broglie wavelength
1 : 2√2, as alpha's larger mass-charge product gives it a longer wavelength
2 : 1, which equals the square root of the alpha-to-proton mass ratio alone

questions.explanation: Using λ = h/√(2mqV): λ_p/λ_α = √(m_α · q_α) / √(m_p · q_p) = √(4m · 2e) / √(m · e) = √8 = 2√2. Option C inverts the ratio — a mistake made when students confuse λ ∝ √(mq) with λ ∝ 1/√(mq). Option D ignores the charge difference between proton (e) and alpha (2e).

questions.stem: If the uncertainty in the position of an electron is 1×10⁻¹⁰ m, the minimum uncertainty in its velocity is closest to? (m_e = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s)

options.option_text: approximately 1.16×10⁶ m/s, derived using the formula Δv ≥ h/(2πmΔx)
approximately 5.8×10⁵ m/s, derived using the formula Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx)
approximately 2.9×10⁵ m/s, treating the minimum as Δv ≥ h/(8πmΔx) form
approximately 3.6×10⁶ m/s, derived by equating kinetic energy to hν/Δx value

questions.explanation: Heisenberg's principle: Δx·Δp ≥ h/(4π). So Δv ≥ h/(4π·m·Δx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ / (4×3.14×9.1×10⁻³¹×10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.8×10⁵ m/s. Option A uses h/(2πmΔx), which is off by a factor of 2 — the common error of using the Bohr quantisation formula instead of the uncertainty relation. Option C halves the correct answer, reflecting use of an h/(8π) form that has no physical basis.

questions.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from the 5th energy level to the 2nd energy level. The emitted photon belongs to which spectral line and region of the electromagnetic spectrum?

options.option_text: Hα line at approximately 656 nm, lying in the red region of visible spectrum
Hγ line at approximately 434 nm, lying in the violet region of visible spectrum
Hβ line at approximately 486 nm, lying in the blue-green region of visible spectrum
Hδ line at approximately 410 nm, lying in the deep violet region of visible spectrum

questions.explanation: All transitions ending at n=2 belong to the Balmer series. The Greek-letter labels are assigned in order of increasing energy: Hα (3→2, 656 nm), Hβ (4→2, 486 nm), Hγ (5→2, 434 nm), Hδ (6→2, 410 nm). Using 1/λ = R_H(1/4 − 1/25) = 21R_H/100 gives λ ≈ 434 nm (violet), confirming Hγ. Option C (Hβ) is the most tempting error — candidates confuse the 4→2 and 5→2 transitions.
